GGIR is a complex software with hundreds of potential use cases. We have various measures in place to monitor functional consistency, but just like any other complex software project it is hard to make this 100% error proof. The best solution is to have a critical and pro-active user community to spot and fix issues quickly.

Researching the cause behind specific changes in output for specific files between specific versions of GGIR is time consuming. I am happy to do this for you as a paid consultancy. GGIR may be for free, but my time is not.

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: Diurnal inactivity: dur_TINday_min in part5
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Re: Diurnal inactivity: dur_TINday_min in part5
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dora,

This is not a bug. If a a person goes to sleep after midnight and wakes up before noon then the date shown in part 5 is the date on which that sleep window started. If that same person then falls asleep before midnight later that day then also that WW window (next line) is timestamped on the same date. I do this day windows are defined based on waking up times and not based on calendar dates. So, expressing recording days relative to a sequence of calendar dates would not be logical. In the MM analysis where days are defined based on calendar dates the dates should however be a displayed in a logical sequence.

A consequence of this is that days can last much shorter or longer than 24 hours. If you encounter such a day I suggest that you inspect the visualisation of the time series for that person. For individuals with irregular sleep/wake rhythms like shift workers it is not uncommon to see highly irregular day lengths in the WW output. GGIR should have enough measures in place to distinguish true behaviour from measurement artifacts.

If despite this visual check you do not trust the output then you could decide to exclude the specific day(s) for specific recording(s) with argument data_cleaning_file.

Thanks,
Vincent

messages.body_plain:
> I am comparing Actiwatch data with Verisense.  Whether there’s an option to increase the sensitivity of it so that the peaks of the data match with  Actiwatch?

GGIR offers the choice between a number of acceleration metrics and connected parameters, some may be more similar to what Actiwatch does with its data than others. I do not know which metric/parameter combination is best to imitate Actiwatch data. I believe there is literature on this. I am happy to investigate this for you as a paid consultancy.

> Also, there seems a delay between ActiWatch and Verisense. Whether there are some data points missing for Verisense, or of there’s a sync issue between both sets of data.

GGIR intentionally starts at an integer number of large epochs (default length is 15 minutes) relative to the hour to ease interpretation and comparison of results across individuals. So, if your recording was started at 8:54 then you will see output from 9:00 onward. This means that when you compare with Actiwatch data always align the data based on timestamps. Needless to say that I do not know how time is handled in Actiwatch software, so it is always good to double check synchronisation visually at multiple time points in the recordings.

Best,
Vincent

to .wav files using omconvert. I was wondering if anyone could advise what’s
the reason behind this? As far as I looked into GGIR guideline, it can resample
and auto-calibrate the input raw signal.

script for analysing the AX3 data. I was wondering if anyone has any suggestions/experience

timewindow = c("WW"),

#=====================

dofirstpage = TRUE,

visualreport=TRUE)

Kind regards,

Mahnoosh

The time is expressed as hours relative to preceding midnight to make it consistent with how numeric times are expressed for sleep onset and waking up time.  So. 26 corresponds to 1.00 AM, and 37 corresponds to 1pm.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manoosh,

"I am trying to extract sleep measures from UK BioBank raw accelerometer data (AX3) using GGIR package (v2.1-0). I came across couple of papers and also some posts in this group, in which it is recommended to first convert .cwa files to .wav files using omconvert. I was wondering if anyone could advise what’s the reason behind this? As far as I looked into GGIR guideline, it can resample and auto-calibrate the input raw signal."

I implemented wav-format compatibility around 2015-2016. Functionality to handle cwa data was added a few years later by Evgeny and in January 2020 I made further improvements to that. However, recently it was discovered that there might be a minor offset in the data for cwa when it comes from older AX3 devices used in UK Biobank. devices: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/issues/369. I do not think this is a major issue, but it would be good if this was investigated and resolved.

I have not worked with the wav-format data since we introduced the cwa read functionality. I am happy to investigate and try to improve both cwa and wav-format compatibility as a paid consultancy. On the other hand, if anyone else wants to investigate this and make a pull request than that is also fine.

"Also, I am new to sleep research and using the following script for analyzing the AX3 data. I was wondering if anyone has any suggestions/experience for parameter setup on this dataset? Any input would be highly appreciated."

I believe Sam Jones shared his R scripts in supplementary file data 10 to our manuscript: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-09576-1 Best advise is probably to dive into the package documentation and familiarise yourself with all function arguments used. If you encounter any issue then let me know.

Best,
Vincent

On Thursday, September 24, 2015 at 4:16:25 PM UTC+1 Godbole, Suneeta wrote:
> Thanks for clarification! As long as the timestamp isn't miss representing the epoch I'm okay with missing the first 15 minutes on the first day.
>
> Thanks again!
> Suni
>
> -----Original Message-----
> From: Vincent van Hees [mailto:vincent...@gmail.com]
> Sent: Thursday, September 24, 2015 5:33 AM
> To: Godbole, Suneeta
> Cc: R package GGIR
> Subject: Re: [GGIR] desiredtz
>
> Hi Sunni,
>
> When data is summarised per epoch the epochs are not relative to the start of the measurement but relative to specific seconds in a minute or minutes in an hour. For example, a 15 minute epoch will always start at 00, 15, 30, or 45 minutes past the hour. I do this to allow for standardised comparison between days and person. So, if a measurement starts at 6 minutes past the hour then the first 9 minutes of the measurement are ignored such that the first recorded epoch starts at 15 minutes past the hour and ends at 30 minutes past the hour.
>
> In your situation the code is undesirably doing something similar. It does not recognise that you have a complete first 15 minutes, but probably thinks that you have 14 minutes and 59 seconds, which makes that those first block of data is not considered. This is obviously a bug.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Vincent
>
> On 23 September 2015 at 22:18, Godbole, Suneeta <sgod...@ucsd.edu> wrote:
> > Hi Vincent,
> >
> > Thanks for the quick and in-depth response. I'm comparing a minute level output from GGIR to minute-level count data and for some odd reason I'm seeing a 15-minute delay from GGIR, what I mean is that the initialization time and first outputted data minute from GGIR have a 15 minute difference (the device is initialized for 12:00 pm and the GGIR output starts at 12:15). Do you have any ideas for why that would be happening? I just want to make sure that the timestamp isn't off by 15 minutes.
> >
> > Thanks!
> > Suni
> > -----Original Message-----
> > From: Vincent van Hees [mailto:vincent...@gmail.com]
> > Sent: Tuesday, September 22, 2015 12:43 AM
> > To: Godbole, Suneeta
> > Cc: R package GGIR
> > Subject: Re: [GGIR] desiredtz
> >
> > Hi Suni,
> >
> > Timestamps are used to identify midnights and by that to identify the time window of a day, to label the summary data with correct dates and to capture the starting time of the measurement. The timestamps are not used for any other aspect of the analyses.
> >
> > Timestamps formats are unfortunately different between accelerometer brands/versions (Genea, Geneactiv, Actigraph) by which I had to come up with a generic piece of code to account for all possible situations (timezones and day saving time). I first made sure that the timestamps are correctly interpreted for the study data I have been working on myself and then only did a few tests with data from other timezones to verify this.
> >
> > It would be good if someone could critically review the timestamp interpretation across accelerometer brands and identify where things might go wrong.
> > I will try to look at this myself, but this could take a while.
> >
> > Please note that if you compare your data with a second piece of software then time may be interpreted differently by that other software. My code relies on the sample frequency in combination with the first timestamp while other software may rely on timestamps.
> > Sample frequency and timestamps are generated by a separate digital clock. At the time I developed the code the Geneactiv accelerometer had an unreliable clock for generating timestamps and an (on average) reliable clock for generating sample frequency, which was why I relied on sample frequency for describing time.
> >
> > Thanks for raising the issue,
> >
